authorRole: Head of Procurement at a multi-speciality hospital chain
post:
A request to every vendor who visits us for the annual rate-contract review: please don't send your managing director.

I appreciate the courtesy. But the MD does not know that our ICU nurses stopped using your surface wipes in March because the canister lid cracks after a week. He does not know that our sterile services head has been asking for a smaller pack size for two years. He arrives with a presentation on the company's growth and a 4% price increase.

The vendors we have kept for ten years send someone who has walked our wards. That person usually knows our consumption better than our own stores team does. When they ask for an increase, they can show what they have saved us in wastage or complaints, and the conversation is short.

We will spend roughly ₹40 crore on consumables across our hospitals this year. I would happily pay a little more to a supplier who understands where it goes.

To sales leaders in this space: who do you send to your biggest renewal, and why?

authorRole: Founder of a sales consultancy for medical device companies
post:
Unpopular opinion: the field sales rep in hospital consumables has five years left.

Here is my reasoning. Large hospital groups now buy through annual tenders and e-procurement portals. Pricing is fixed for twelve months. Product specifications are written by a committee. Once the contract is signed, the rep who visits the ward every week has very little left to influence.

Meanwhile, a field rep in a metro city, with travel, now costs ₹12–15 lakh a year. Many companies I advise carry teams of 80 or 100 people whose main activity is checking stock and collecting outstanding payments.

The smarter companies are already moving to a small key-account team for the big groups, inside sales for smaller nursing homes, and clinical specialists who are measured on training, not orders.

I know this will upset some people. I spent fourteen years carrying a bag myself. But I think we owe our teams an honest conversation about where the job is going, rather than pretending the 2015 model still works.

Am I wrong? I would genuinely like to hear from people running hospital sales teams today.

authorRole: Regional Sales Manager at a diagnostics company
post:
Sales is not a job. It is a mindset. 💯

After 11 years in sales, here is what I have learned about top performers:

1. They wake up before everyone else.
2. They never take no for an answer.
3. They treat every customer like family.
4. They are hungry, always.
5. They don't make excuses, they make results.

Talent is overrated. Attitude is everything. The difference between a good salesperson and a great one is not skill, it is the fire inside.

I tell my team every Monday: the market does not owe you anything. Go out and take what is yours. Rejection is just redirection. Every no brings you closer to a yes.

To all the warriors in the field doing the hard work in the heat and the traffic, I see you. Keep pushing. Your time is coming. 🔥🔥

Agree? Drop a 🙌 if you are a sales warrior!

#Sales #Motivation #SalesLeadership #Hustle #Mindset

authorRole: Chief Nursing Officer at a 600-bed teaching hospital
post:
We audited hand-hygiene compliance on 14 wards for six months. The biggest improvement had nothing to do with the product.

At the start, observed compliance before patient contact was 58%. We had already changed suppliers once, on the promise that a better-tolerated hand rub would fix it. It did not.

What moved the number was where the dispensers were. On most wards they were mounted at the entrance, which is where the architect put them, not at the bedside, which is where care happens. When our infection-control nurses moved dispensers to within arm's reach of each bed and added one to every medication trolley, compliance rose to 81% in ten weeks.

Two other small things helped: refilling on a fixed schedule, so no one met an empty dispenser at 3am, and letting ward sisters, not managers, run the observations.

I share this because vendors still come to us with product features. I would rather talk to a supplier who has walked our wards and can tell me where the gaps are.

Has anyone else seen placement matter more than product?

authorRole: Managing Director of a pharmaceutical and surgical distribution company
post:
From April, our sales organisation will move from territories to accounts.

For twenty years we have organised by geography: a manager for each region, reps for each city, targets by pin code. It worked when our customers were thousands of independent nursing homes and chemists. Today, seven hospital groups account for nearly 40% of our institutional revenue, and each of them buys centrally.

So we are creating a key-account team of nine people for those groups, each responsible for one group across every city it operates in. The regional teams will focus on independent hospitals and clinics, where local relationships still decide everything.

We know what can go wrong. Reps who have looked after a hospital for a decade may feel we are taking their best customer away. Incentives will need to be shared during the transition, and we have not got that fully right yet. Some regional managers will see their numbers shrink on paper.

We have spent four months consulting the team and will review the design after two quarters.

If you have made this shift in a sales team, I would value your advice, particularly on how you handled incentives in the first year.

authorRole: CTO at a Series B fintech startup
post:
We removed product engineers from on-call six months ago. Best decision I have made as CTO.

Here is what we did. A dedicated reliability team of seven now carries every page, day and night. Product squads hand over services with runbooks and dashboards, and the reliability team can roll back any deploy without asking.

The results so far: feature throughput, measured by merged pull requests per engineer per week, is up by about 30%. Engineers report better sleep in our pulse survey. Attrition among product engineers is the lowest it has been.

I know the "you build it, you run it" crowd will say this creates a wall between the people who write code and the people who feel the pain. Maybe. But I would rather have specialists who are excellent at incident response than eighty developers who are mediocre at it and resent every rotation.

The trade-offs we accept: the reliability team has to be staffed properly and rotated carefully to avoid burnout, and product teams must fix the issues it raises within an agreed time.

Curious how other engineering leaders think about this. Is "you build it, you run it" still the right default at our size?

authorRole: Staff Engineer at a logistics software company
post:
Last month a one-line configuration change took our checkout API down for 47 minutes during peak hours.

The change was reviewed and approved. It lowered a connection pool limit that looked oversized. Nobody knew that a batch job, owned by another team, relied on that headroom every evening at 7pm.

The technical fixes were straightforward: config changes now go through the same staged rollout as code, and pool limits alert at 80%.

The harder lesson was about the first hour after recovery. A senior manager joined the incident channel and asked, three times, who made the change. The engineer who did it went quiet, and so did everyone else. We lost the most useful information we had, which was how the change looked reasonable to everyone at the time.

In the postmortem, our VP opened by saying the system had made this easy to get wrong, and that the question was how. The engineer then walked us through exactly what she had checked and why the dependency was invisible. That led to our best action item: a dependency map for shared configuration.

Blameless postmortems are not about being kind. They are about getting the truth while it is still available.

authorRole: Engineering Manager at a developer tools startup
post:
Question for engineering leaders at mid-size companies: how do you define "senior" versus "staff" without copying a big-tech ladder?

We are about 60 engineers. Until now, titles were informal, and that worked while everyone knew everyone. Now people are asking, fairly, what it takes to get promoted, and two of our managers would give very different answers.

I have read the published ladders from much larger companies. They are thorough, and they describe organisations with hundreds of teams, cross-org initiatives and dedicated architecture groups. Half of the "staff" examples simply do not exist at our scale.

What I am leaning towards: senior engineers own a system and the decisions inside it; staff engineers own decisions that cross systems or teams, and are judged on whether those decisions hold up a year later. Fewer levels, clearer examples, and a promotion case made mostly of written decisions rather than a list of projects.

What I am unsure about: whether staff should require influence beyond their own team at our size, and how to avoid creating a title people chase rather than a role they grow into.

If you have built a ladder for a 50–150 person engineering org, what did you get wrong the first time?

authorRole: VP Engineering at a healthtech SaaS company
post:
We tracked our delivery metrics for twelve months. Getting faster made us less stable before it made us more stable.

From January to June we moved to trunk-based development and smaller pull requests. Deployment frequency went from about 3 a week to 11 a week. Lead time for changes dropped from 6 days to under 2.

But our change failure rate rose from 9% to 14% over the same period. More deploys, more small breakages. A couple of senior engineers argued that we should slow down again.

We did not. We added contract tests to the three services that caused most failures, made feature flags the default for anything customer-facing, and asked every team to review its own failed changes once a month.

By December, change failure rate was down to 6%, and mean time to restore was under 30 minutes, from about 2 hours.

My takeaway: the speed-versus-stability trade-off is real in the short term. It goes away only if you invest in the safety net while you speed up, not after.

I'd be interested to hear whether others saw the same dip, and how long it lasted.

authorRole: Founder of a tech hiring agency
post:
Hard truth: AI will replace junior developers by 2027. 🤖

I have spoken to dozens of CTOs this year. Every single one says the same thing. Why hire three freshers when one senior engineer with AI tools can do the work of five?

The writing is on the wall. Coding is becoming a commodity. The developers who survive will be the ones who adapt, upskill and become AI-first.

If you are a junior developer reading this, don't panic. But don't be complacent either. Learn prompt engineering. Build projects. Network like your career depends on it, because it does.

Companies that still run large fresher hiring programmes are living in the past. The future belongs to small, elite teams.

Adapt or get left behind. The choice is yours. 🚀

authorRole: CFO of a listed engineering goods manufacturer
post:
Two years ago our month-end close took nine working days. Last month it took four. Technology was perhaps a fifth of the improvement.

What made the difference:

We moved accruals and provisions to a rolling calendar, so most judgement calls are made in the third week of the month, not the first week of the next.

We gave every balance sheet account a single owner, including the ones that had been "shared" between plants and head office for years. Shared ownership had meant no ownership.

We stopped producing eleven versions of the management pack. There is now one, and plant heads see it at the same time as the board does.

We agreed with our statutory auditors which schedules they would receive and when, so the team was not rebuilding reports in a hurry every quarter.

The ERP upgrade helped, but only after these changes. Had we automated the old process, we would simply have had a faster mess.

For finance leaders in manufacturing: what has made the biggest difference to your close that was not a system?

authorRole: Audit partner at a mid-size chartered accountancy firm
post:
After twenty audit seasons, the issue I raise most often with manufacturing clients is not fraud or complex accounting. It is inventory provisioning decided in the last week.

The pattern is familiar. Slow-moving and obsolete stock is reviewed once a quarter by the central finance team, using an ageing report. The plant teams, who know which parts will never be used again because a vehicle programme has ended, are not in the room. The provision is a percentage applied by age bucket, and it is debated with the auditors under deadline.

The better companies I audit do three things differently. They review slow-moving stock monthly with the plant and the programme managers. They document why an item is not obsolete, not just why it is. And they link provisioning to customer programme end dates, which are usually known well in advance.

The result is fewer surprises in the fourth quarter and a much shorter conversation with us.

I would encourage audit committee members to ask one question: who outside finance has seen the inventory provision before it reaches the auditors?

authorRole: Head of Treasury at an auto-components supplier
post:
We reduced our receivable days from 72 to 58 in a year. The single biggest change was who gets rewarded for collecting cash.

Until last year, our sales team's incentive was based entirely on invoiced revenue. Collection was finance's problem. Our sales managers had strong relationships with customers' purchase departments but almost never spoke to their accounts payable teams.

We changed the incentive so that 30% of it depends on collections within agreed terms. We also gave each sales manager a weekly view of overdue invoices by customer, with the reason for each delay.

Two things surprised us. First, a large share of delays were caused by our own errors: wrong PO references, missing proof of delivery, prices that did not match the latest agreement. Sales could fix most of those with one phone call. Second, customers responded better to a sales manager raising a dispute than to a reminder from finance.

Not everyone liked it. Two senior salespeople argued that collections were outside their control, and in a few cases they were right.

I am curious: do other manufacturers link sales incentives to cash, and how do you handle the cases that really are outside sales' control?

authorRole: Plant Head at an auto-components manufacturer
post:
Honest observation after 22 years on the shop floor: most finance teams have never seen the process they are reporting on.

Every month we receive an MIS pack that tells us what happened five weeks ago. Scrap is up. Overtime is up. Power cost per unit is up. By the time it reaches me, my production managers already know, because they lived it.

Meanwhile, finance asks us to explain variances in a template that has not changed in eight years, using cost centres that do not match how the plant actually runs. So my team keeps its own spreadsheets, and in every review we argue about whose number is right instead of what to do about it.

I am not saying finance is not needed. A good controller has saved me more than once, by spotting supplier price creep we had missed. But that controller came and stood on the line with us for a week before she built a single report.

If finance wants to be a business partner, start by walking the plant. Learn what a changeover is. Then design the report.

Maybe this is unfair to some of you. Finance leaders, tell me where I am wrong.

authorRole: Chief Operating Officer at a mutual building society
post:
We switched off our old mainframe last month, five years after we started replacing it. A few things I would tell myself at the beginning.

First, the data migration is the programme. We spent two years designing the new platform and treated migration as a workstream. It should have been the other way round. Every serious delay we had came from data nobody understood, held in fields that had been used for three different purposes since the 1990s.

Second, keep the people who know the old system close and valued. We nearly lost two engineers who had maintained the mainframe for decades because they felt they were being retired with it. Without them, we would not have understood half of what we were migrating.

Third, do not go big bang. We moved members in tranches of about 30,000, starting with the simplest savings accounts. The first tranche found 140 issues. The last found two.

Fourth, tell the board early what will not be ready. Their patience was much greater when they heard bad news from us first.

The programme ran a year longer than planned. I am still proud of how it ended.

If you are about to start one of these, I am happy to share more.

authorRole: Customer experience consultant and former contact centre director
post:
I listened to 2,000 complaint calls across three UK lenders over the past year. Thirty-eight per cent were caused by the lender's own letters.

Not by a product failure. Not by a system outage. By a letter that was accurate, compliant and impossible to understand.

The common patterns: a statement that shows a balance going up when the customer has just made a payment, with no explanation. A payment-change letter where the new monthly amount is on page three. A "we need more information" letter that does not say what information.

In each case, the contact centre had flagged the problem. The feedback went into a log, the log went to a committee, and the letter belonged to a team in a different building that was measured on compliance sign-off, not on the calls it generated.

The fix is usually cheap. One lender rewrote four letters with contact centre staff in the room and saw calls on those topics fall by more than half within two months.

So my question for operations and change leaders: in your organisation, who owns the letters? And are they measured on what the letters cause?

authorRole: Chief Digital Officer at a challenger bank
post:
Uncomfortable view: incumbent banks should stop trying to transform their legacy estate. It cannot be done at an acceptable cost.

I spent twelve years inside two large banks before joining a challenger. In both, "transformation" meant layering new apps on top of core systems from the 1980s, wrapped in middleware nobody fully understood. Each programme delivered a nicer front end and a more fragile back end.

The alternative is to build a new bank alongside the old one, on modern infrastructure, with its own licence if necessary, and migrate customers product by product. Then switch the old estate off.

Yes, it is expensive. Yes, you run two banks for years. But compare that with the cumulative cost of ten years of programmes that each claimed to modernise and each left the core untouched.

The objections I hear are usually about risk and regulatory appetite. I think the bigger risk is spending another decade pretending.

Transformation leaders in established banks: is a parallel build realistic, or am I underestimating what it takes?

authorRole: Interim programme director in financial services change
post:
Question for people who lead change in large organisations: how do you know, twelve months later, whether a change actually stuck?

I have closed a lot of programmes. Every one ended with a benefits realisation report. Most of those reports were written by the programme team, using numbers chosen by the programme team, a month before the programme team disbanded. I am not proud of all of them.

What I have seen work, occasionally:

A named business owner who inherits the benefit and is still accountable for it a year later, in their own objectives.

A small set of operational measures agreed before go-live, owned by the operational team rather than reported by the programme.

A return visit at six and twelve months, where someone simply watches how the process runs today and compares it with the design.

The most honest test I know is whether staff have quietly built workarounds. If they have, the change has not stuck, whatever the report says.

What do you use? I am especially interested in approaches that survive the programme team leaving.

authorRole: Chief Executive of a regional building society
post:
This weekend we moved our last 410,000 members onto our new savings and mortgage platform.

It is the end of a journey that started in 2021, and I want to say thank you.

To our technology and operations teams, who worked through three bank holiday weekends this year so that members would notice as little as possible.

To our branch colleagues, who answered every question patiently in the weeks before the switch, and who flagged problems with the new screens that saved us from much worse ones later.

To our members, who put up with letters, password resets and the occasional queue.

We did not get everything right. Our first migration weekend in March ran eleven hours over, and some members could not see their balances on the Monday morning. We apologised, paused, and changed the plan. Every weekend after that was smoother.

The new platform means we can open an account in minutes rather than days, and change a product without a six-month IT project.

But the real test starts now: whether, in a year's time, our colleagues say the new way of working is simply how we do things.

authorRole: Consultant in emergency medicine and clinical safety officer
post:
Every digital system I have seen introduced in fifteen years has added clicks. I cannot think of one that took any away.

A new sepsis screening tool: four extra fields per patient. A new falls assessment: a mandatory pop-up at triage. A new discharge summary template: three more screens before the letter can be sent. Each was justified on its own terms. Each was signed off by a committee that did not have to complete it at 3am with a corridor full of patients.

Suppliers measure success by features delivered and modules live. Programme boards measure go-live dates. Nobody I know measures clinician time per patient before and after.

I would like to see one simple rule: no new mandatory field unless an existing one is removed, or someone can show that the time it takes is justified by what it prevents.

I am not against digital. Our electronic prescribing system has prevented errors I would rather not think about. But we have to start treating clinicians' time as the scarcest resource in the building.

Has anyone actually managed to remove clicks from a clinical system? I would love to hear how.

authorRole: Chief Nursing Information Officer at an acute hospital trust
post:
Today we completed the rollout of electronic observations across all 24 adult inpatient wards. 🎉

Eighteen months ago our nurses were recording vital signs on paper charts, calculating early warning scores by hand, and phoning doctors when a patient deteriorated. Now observations go straight into the record from handheld devices, scores are calculated automatically, and the outreach team is alerted in real time.

Some early numbers: observations completed on time have gone from 71% to 93% on the pilot wards. The average time from a high score to a clinical review has fallen from 48 minutes to 19.

None of this happened because of the technology alone. Our ward champions, one or two nurses on every ward, tested every screen, trained their colleagues on nights and weekends, and told us bluntly when something did not work. We redesigned the observation screen three times because of them.

There were hard moments. Wi-Fi black spots on two wards meant devices dropped out mid-entry, and we had to pause go-live there for six weeks.

Thank you to everyone who stuck with it. Next: paediatrics.

authorRole: Founder of a patient booking and reminders start-up
post:
Honest question for anyone who has sold software into hospital trusts: how long did your first procurement take?

We started conversations with our first trust 14 months ago. Clinical teams love the product. We ran a pilot in two outpatient clinics that cut missed appointments by about a fifth. The divisional director wants it.

Since then we have completed an information governance assessment, a clinical safety case, a data protection impact assessment, a cyber security questionnaire, a value-for-money review and two rounds of commercial clarification. Each step was reasonable. Each took longer than the last, partly because the people involved also have day jobs.

We are a team of nine. We have enough runway to keep going, but I am starting to wonder whether we should sell through larger suppliers instead of directly.

I am not complaining; I understand why the safeguards exist. I would just like to know what normal looks like, and what the founders who got through it did differently.

If you have been on either side of this, buyer or supplier, I would genuinely value your view.

authorRole: Head of Patient Experience at a community health service
post:
Before building our new online patient portal, we asked 312 patients and carers what they wanted from it. The top answer surprised our whole programme board.

We expected booking appointments to come first. It came fourth.

The top answer, from 61% of respondents, was "knowing who to contact". People with long-term conditions are often seen by four or five different teams: district nurses, physiotherapy, a specialist nurse, their GP practice. When something changes, they do not know who to call, so they call everyone, or no one.

Second was seeing upcoming visits in one place. Third was being able to tell us about a change, such as a hospital admission, without waiting on hold.

We rewrote our first release around those three things. The "my care team" page, which lists every team involved with a named contact and a phone number, is now the most visited page on the portal by a long way.

Booking is coming in the next release. But I am glad we asked before we built.

What has asking patients changed in your own projects?

authorRole: Clinical Director for digital services at a mental health trust
post:
I am going to say something unpopular in my own field: co-design has become theatre.

The pattern goes like this. A programme runs three workshops with patients and staff. There are sticky notes, a large printed journey map, and a lovely photograph for the newsletter. The insights are written up. Then the supplier builds what was already in the contract, because the specification was signed six months before the workshops took place.

Participants notice. Patients who gave up an afternoon to share painful experiences see the final product and recognise nothing of what they said. Staff stop coming to the next round.

Real co-design is slower and less photogenic. It means involving people before the business case is written, giving them a say over what gets cut, and going back to tell them what happened to their ideas, including the ones that were rejected.

I am not arguing against involving patients. I am arguing against calling a consultation exercise co-design, because it devalues the real thing.

Has anyone managed to build genuine co-design into a procurement timeline? I would like to know how.

authorRole: Estate planning attorney
post:
Most of the family disputes I have seen in twenty years of practice started with a plan that was legally perfect.

The trusts were well drafted. The tax analysis was sound. The documents were signed, witnessed and stored safely. And the children found out what was in them at the reading, after their father had died.

One son learned he would be co-trustee with a sister he had not spoken to in years. A daughter who had run the family business for a decade discovered her shares were equal to those of siblings who had never worked there. Nobody had told them why. Their father's reasoning, which was probably fair, died with him.

I now ask every client the same question before we finalize anything: who will be surprised by this plan, and have you told them?

Many clients would rather not. The conversation is uncomfortable. But a hard conversation now is almost always cheaper, financially and emotionally, than litigation later.

For advisors and attorneys who work with families: how do you encourage clients to explain their plans while they still can?

authorRole: Founder of a coaching practice for financial advisors
post:
Controversial view: new advisors should not run client meetings on their own for at least three years.

I know many firms put juniors in front of clients early. The argument is that they learn faster and the firm gets more capacity. I think we underestimate the cost.

A family meeting is not a product presentation. It involves money, grief, sibling rivalries and health scares, often in the same hour. A second-year advisor may know the planning software perfectly and still miss the moment when a client's spouse goes quiet. That moment is often where the real issue sits.

In my old practice, junior advisors sat in on every meeting for their first three years. They took notes, prepared the analysis and debriefed with a senior advisor afterward. Clients got continuity. Juniors saw dozens of difficult conversations before they had to lead one.

The objection I hear is that juniors get bored and leave. Some did. The ones who stayed became excellent.

I would be curious to hear from people who develop advisors today. When is someone ready to lead a family meeting alone, and how do you know?

authorRole: Behavioral economist and university lecturer
post:
New paper from our lab, and a finding I think advisors will find useful.

We followed 1,180 individual investors over four years. At the start, half were asked to write a short statement explaining the purpose of their savings: what the money was for, when they expected to need it, and what would make them change course. The other half received the same information but were not asked to write anything.

During periods of sharp market decline, the group who had written a statement were significantly less likely to make large, unplanned changes to their allocation. The effect was strongest among people who had written in their own words, rather than ticking boxes on a form, and among those who were reminded of what they had written.

We think the mechanism is simple. A written purpose gives people something to return to when their emotions are telling them to act.

What we could not measure is how advisors use this in practice. Some told us they already do something similar in client reviews.

If you advise families, do you ask clients to write down their goals in their own words? What happens when you show it to them later?

authorRole: Second-generation owner of a family manufacturing business
post:
I need advice from people who have been through this.

My father founded our company 46 years ago. He is 74, still comes in every day, and still signs every check over a certain amount. My brother and I have run operations and sales for more than a decade. We have a capable management team. On paper, there is a succession plan, prepared by our attorneys years ago.

In practice, nobody has ever talked about when it happens. Every time I raise it, my father hears it as "we want you gone," and the conversation ends. My mother quietly takes his side. My brother would rather not rock the boat.

I love my father. I don't want to push him out of something he built with his own hands. But I also know that if something happened to him tomorrow, our bank, our employees and our customers would face months of uncertainty.

For those who have been through it, as founders, children or advisors: how did the conversation actually start? What helped, and what made things worse?

authorRole: Marketing consultant for wealth management firms
post:
Your clients don't care how much you know until they know how much you care. 💙

After working with over 200 advisors, here is the truth: relationships beat returns. Every single time.

Clients don't leave because of performance. They leave because they feel ignored. They leave because nobody called when the market dropped. They leave because their advisor forgot their daughter's name.

The best advisors I know:
✅ Pick up the phone
✅ Remember birthdays
✅ Show up in tough times
✅ Put people before portfolios

In a world of robo-advisors and AI, the human touch is your competitive advantage. Never forget that. The technology will keep changing. What clients want from you will not.

Trust is earned in drops and lost in buckets. 💧

Who agrees? Tag an advisor who puts relationships first! 👇

#WealthManagement #FinancialAdvisor #ClientExperience #Relationships #Trust

authorRole: VP Supply Chain at a consumer packaged goods company
post:
Unpopular opinion: for most mid-size consumer brands, nearshoring is a slide-deck strategy.

We modeled it three times in the past two years, with three different consulting teams. Each time the board was enthusiastic. Each time the landed cost only worked for a handful of SKUs, mostly bulky, low-value items where freight dominates the cost.

For everything else, the savings in transit time and inventory were outweighed by higher unit costs, supplier minimums we could not meet at our volumes, and the cost of qualifying new suppliers. We would have needed two years of dual sourcing to get there safely.

What did work: holding more safety stock on our top 40 items, splitting orders across two existing suppliers in different regions, and shortening our planning cycle from monthly to weekly. Not glamorous, but our fill rate has stayed above 95% through two difficult years.

I'm not saying nearshoring never makes sense. For large brands with scale, it might. But I see a lot of companies chasing the headline instead of doing the math on their own network.

Supply chain leaders: has anyone made it pay for a mid-size portfolio?

authorRole: Operating Partner at a mid-market private equity firm
post:
After eleven acquisitions, I have stopped believing in the 100-day plan as it is usually written.

The plan arrives from the deal team: procurement savings here, pricing actions there, a new ERP by month nine. It is built on diligence data, management presentations and a model that assumes the numbers are right.

In every one of those eleven companies, the first 100 days were mostly spent finding out which numbers were real. Inventory that existed in the system but not in the warehouse. Customer profitability calculated without freight. A "best-in-class" on-time delivery figure that measured promise date against ship date, not delivery.

Now I run the first 60 days differently. Two people from operations and one from finance go to the sites and rebuild, from source, the five numbers the investment case depends on. Only then do we commit to targets.

Management teams were suspicious at first. Several later said it was the most useful thing we did, because it stopped them being held to a plan they knew was wrong.

For operators and advisors: what is the first number you check when you walk into a new business?

authorRole: Director of Distribution Operations at a regional grocery chain
post:
We re-slotted our main distribution center in March. The results were better and messier than I expected.

We moved our top 220 SKUs by pick frequency into the zone closest to the dispatch docks and put the heaviest items at waist height. The design came from a simple velocity analysis, nothing fancy.

After eight weeks:
Pick rate up 18%, measured in cases per labor hour.
Travel distance per order down about a third.
Mis-picks up 6% in the first month, then back to baseline by week seven.

The mis-picks were the surprise. Our experienced pickers knew the old layout by memory. Several said they picked worse because, for the first time in years, they had to think about where things were. Newer staff adapted faster.

If I did it again, I would move in waves rather than over one weekend, and pair veterans with newer pickers for the first two weeks.

The other lesson: velocity changes. Twenty of our "top" SKUs were seasonal and dropped out by June. We now review slotting monthly instead of annually.

Has anyone found a good rhythm for re-slotting without disrupting the floor?

authorRole: Engagement Manager at a boutique strategy firm
post:
A question for consulting leaders: how do you give first-year analysts real client exposure without risking the relationship?

I run small teams, usually three or four people. My analysts are smart and hardworking, and most of them spend their first year building slides that someone else presents. Then, in year two, we put them in front of a COO and expect them to know how to handle pushback.

I have tried a few things. Letting an analyst present one page of a steering committee deck. Having them run a working session with the client's middle managers. Sending them to a plant for a week with a client team.

The plant visits have worked best. The analysts come back with better questions, and the client team usually likes them. The steering committee pages have been mixed: one analyst did brilliantly; another froze when the CFO challenged a number, and I had to step in.

I don't want to protect them so much that they never learn, and I don't want to burn a client relationship for the sake of development.

What has worked for you? And how do you prepare analysts for the moment a senior client disagrees with them?

authorRole: Founder of a supply chain analytics startup
post:
We just published our first annual benchmark on forecast accuracy in mid-size consumer goods companies, and some of the results surprised even us.

We surveyed 146 companies with revenue between $100 million and $2 billion, and analyzed actual forecast and sales data from 38 of them.

A few findings:
Median forecast accuracy at SKU level was 61%. Companies believed, on average, that theirs was around 75%.
Companies that reviewed forecasts weekly were no more accurate than those that reviewed monthly, unless the weekly review included sales and finance.
The biggest gap between the top and bottom quartile was not software. It was whether promotions were planned in the same system as the base forecast.
Fewer than one in five companies tracked forecast value added, meaning whether manual overrides improved the forecast or made it worse.

The full report is free, with no sales follow-up attached. Link in the comments.

We'd love feedback from people who live this every day. What did we miss, and what should we measure next year?

authorRole: Chief Medical Information Officer at a regional health system
post:
A plea to health tech startups: please stop asking me for "a few clinicians who can give some quick feedback."

I get this request about twice a week. It usually means an hour-long video call with a nurse or physician, at the end of a twelve-hour shift, to review screens for a product our health system has not bought and may never buy. There is rarely any payment. Often there is no follow-up.

I understand why you ask. You need clinical input, and you should. But our clinicians' time is the scarcest resource in our building. Every unpaid hour they give you is an hour of rest they don't get.

What works better, from my side:
Pay clinicians fairly for their time, through a proper agreement.
Come to them. Watch a shift, with permission, rather than asking them to describe it on a call.
Tell them what changed because of their feedback.
Ask the people who will use the product, not just the ones with "informatics" in their title.

The startups that do this get our best people coming back to help. The ones that don't quietly stop getting replies.

Founders and product leaders: how do you approach clinician feedback?

authorRole: Head of Regulatory Affairs at a digital therapeutics company
post:
Our first regulatory submission was seven months late. Almost all of the delay came from decisions made two years earlier.

We treated regulatory documentation as something you do at the end. The product team built quickly, made sensible design choices and moved on. When we sat down to write the submission, we had to reconstruct why each requirement existed, which risks each feature addressed, and how we had verified it. Some of that evidence simply did not exist. We had to re-run usability testing because the original sessions had not been documented to the standard required.

On our second product we did it differently. A regulatory specialist joins discovery from week one. Every product requirement is linked to a risk and a verification method when it is written, not later. Design reviews produce a short record that goes straight into the design history file. It adds a little time to each sprint.

The second submission went in on schedule, and the questions we got back were about the science, not the paperwork.

If you are shipping software in a regulated space, the cheapest time to think about evidence is before you build. What has worked for your teams?

authorRole: Senior Product Designer at a telehealth company
post:
Over the last quarter our team spent 40 hours shadowing nurses in three outpatient clinics. Here are five patterns we didn't expect.

1. Nurses keep a paper list in their pocket even when the electronic task list is open on screen. The paper list is faster to update between rooms.
2. The most common workaround was writing on gloves, usually medication times and room numbers.
3. Interruptions averaged one every four minutes. Any flow that took longer than that was usually abandoned and restarted.
4. Nobody used our patient messaging feature during clinic hours. They answered messages in a batch after the last patient, often from home.
5. Senior nurses had built shortcuts that juniors didn't know existed. Knowledge spread by word of mouth, not training.

The biggest change for us: we now design for interruption. Every task has to survive being left halfway through and picked up again by someone else.

We also dropped two roadmap items that solved problems nobody in the clinic actually had.

If you design for clinicians, what's the most surprising thing you've seen while shadowing?

authorRole: Founder and CEO of a seed-stage clinical workflow startup
post:
Hot take: product managers in healthtech don't need clinical backgrounds. In fact, I think hiring clinicians as PMs often slows teams down.

I've hired both. Former nurses and physicians bring credibility and deep domain knowledge. But in my experience, they also tend to design for the way they practiced, in their specialty, at their hospital. Their instincts are strong, so they test them less.

PMs without clinical backgrounds know what they don't know. They go and watch. They ask clinicians to explain things a former nurse would assume. Some of our best discovery came from a PM who had never set foot on a ward and asked "why do you do it that way?" fifty times in one shift.

What we do instead: PMs from a product background, paired with paid clinical advisors from several care settings, plus a clinical safety lead with real authority to stop a release.

I know this will annoy some people, and I may be generalizing from a small sample. But I'd rather have a team that is curious than one that is certain.

Product leaders in health: who do you hire, and why?

authorRole: Agile coach and keynote speaker
post:
Fail fast. Learn faster. 🚀

The best product teams I've worked with all have one thing in common: psychological safety.

When people feel safe to take risks, innovation happens. When they're afraid to fail, nothing changes.

Here's the truth most leaders don't want to hear: your team isn't underperforming. Your culture is.

Great product cultures:
💡 Celebrate failure
💡 Empower teams
💡 Embrace experimentation
💡 Put the customer at the center
💡 Never stop learning

Remember: done is better than perfect. Progress over perfection. Every failure is a lesson in disguise. The teams that win are not the ones that never fall. They're the ones that get back up faster.

If you're a leader, ask yourself today: is my team safe to fail?

authorRole: Founder of a direct-to-consumer skincare brand
post:
Founders, I would love some advice on a decision I keep putting off.

We are three years in, with annual revenue of around AED 18 million, mostly online across the UAE and Saudi Arabia, plus two retail partners. Our marketing is currently run by me, a brand manager, a performance marketing agency and a separate creative agency.

It has worked so far. But growth has slowed this year, the two agencies blame each other for results, and I am spending far more time on marketing than on product or partnerships.

The options on the table:
Hire a full-time CMO, which is a big commitment at our stage.
Bring in a fractional CMO for 12 months to set strategy and build the team.
Keep the agencies and hire a strong marketing manager to coordinate them.

My worry with a full-time hire is that we choose the wrong person and lose a year. My worry with the fractional route is that nobody owns execution once they leave.

If you have been here, what did you choose, and what would you do differently? I am especially interested in hearing from consumer brands in the region.

authorRole: Marketing Director at a boutique hotel group
post:
Last year we cut our paid social budget by 40% and moved the money into guest research and our own CRM. Direct bookings rose by 22%.

Some context. Like most hotel groups, we were spending heavily on social ads to drive awareness, then paying booking platforms a large commission on the guests who actually came. Our marketing reports looked healthy: reach, impressions, engagement. Our margins did not.

We took about half of the paid social budget and used it to interview 60 past guests and survey around 1,500 more. The most useful finding was that repeat guests chose us for the staff and the neighbourhood, not the rooms, which our ads had featured almost exclusively.

We rebuilt our messaging around that, and used the rest of the money to fix our CRM so we could email past guests with something relevant rather than generic offers.

Paid social still matters for new markets. But for our existing audience, knowing them better was worth more than reaching more of them.

Has anyone else shifted budget from reach to research? I'd be interested to compare notes.

authorRole: Brand strategist at a creative agency
post:
Unpopular opinion from someone who earns money from them: most rebrands are a confession.

They confess that the company does not know what it stands for, and hopes a new logo will tell it.

I have worked on more than thirty rebrands. In my experience, fewer than a third were needed. The rest were triggered by a new CEO who wanted a visible early win, a marketing team bored with its own identity long before customers were, or slowing growth that nobody wanted to diagnose properly.

The tell is the brief. A good rebrand brief starts with a change in strategy: new customers, a new category, a merger. A bad one starts with "we feel dated" and a mood board.

The costs are real. Not just agency fees, but signage, packaging, retraining staff, and the recognition you have spent years building.

When a client asks me for a rebrand now, I ask what they would change if they could not touch the logo. If they cannot answer, we are not ready to talk about design.

Marketers and founders: have you seen a rebrand that was a genuine turning point? What made it work?

authorRole: Head of Sales at a residential property developer
post:
Our best-selling launch last year had the smallest marketing budget we have ever had.

Here is what we did differently. Before the architects finalised the floor plans, our sales team interviewed 50 people who had bought from us in the previous two years, plus around 30 people who had visited our show apartments and not bought.

We learned things no market report had told us. Families wanted a separate space for a home office far more than a larger balcony. Buyers with young children cared more about where the lifts opened than about the gym. Several people who did not buy said our payment plans were confusing, not expensive.

We changed the layouts of two unit types, simplified the payment plan to three options, and built the marketing around the home office and the family layout.

The launch sold out in five weeks, with roughly half our usual advertising spend.

The lesson for me was that marketing works much harder when the product already matches what people want. Research is cheaper than persuasion.

Has anyone else brought customer research into product design this early in property?

authorRole: Health and safety consultant to construction contractors
post:
I will say it plainly: "zero harm" targets are making some sites less safe.

I understand the intention. Nobody should be hurt at work. But when a zero-incident target is tied to bonuses, league tables and client scorecards, the message on site is not "be safe". It is "do not report".

I see the evidence on almost every audit. Projects with the best incident statistics often have the thinnest near-miss logs. First aid cases are recorded as "no treatment required". Workers with minor injuries are quietly moved to light duties so the lost-time figure stays clean.

The projects I would actually trust have more reports, not fewer. Their supervisors are praised for raising concerns. Their near-miss boards are full, and visibly acted on.

My suggestion to project owners and contractors: stop rewarding the absence of incidents. Reward the quality of reporting and the speed of closing actions. Measure leading indicators, not just lagging ones.

I expect pushback on this, and I welcome it. But I have seen too many "zero harm" banners at the gates of sites where people were afraid to speak.

authorRole: Commercial Director at a main contractor
post:
The project that ended best for us commercially was not the one with the best contract. It was the one where we recorded everything within 24 hours.

On most large projects, disputes over variations come down to evidence: who instructed what, when, and with what consequences. By the time a claim is prepared, the site team has moved on, the diary entries are thin, and the engineer who received the instruction has left the project.

On this job we set a simple rule from the first week. Every instruction, whether written, verbal or given in a site meeting, was logged in a shared register within 24 hours, with a photo or a sketch where possible, and the register was acknowledged by the client's representative every week.

It felt bureaucratic at first, and our site engineers complained. But when the final account came, there was very little to argue about. Most variations were agreed in a few meetings, not months of correspondence.

The relationship with the client also improved, because neither side was storing up surprises.

I now think good records are less about protecting yourself and more about making honest agreement possible.

authorRole: Planning Manager on a metro rail project
post:
We analysed 18 months of schedule data on our project to understand what was really driving critical-path delays. The answer was not what our monthly reports suggested.

Our reports usually attributed delays to the obvious events: late material deliveries, weather, a utility diversion that took longer than planned.

When we went through every delay event on the critical path, 64% traced back to design information, specifically requests for information that went unanswered for more than seven days. Individually, none of them looked serious. A missing dimension. An unclear detail at an interface. Collectively, they cost us more time than everything else combined.

Two changes have made a difference since. We now track the age of every open request daily, and anything older than five days is raised at the morning coordination meeting with the design manager present. And we pair each site package with a named designer who can answer simple queries by phone.

Average response time has fallen from eleven days to four.

I would be interested to know whether other planners see the same pattern on their projects, and what has worked to speed up design responses.

authorRole: Site engineer, three years into a construction career
post:
A question for experienced project and construction leaders.

I am three years into my career as a site engineer. I have worked on a residential tower and now on a highway interchange. I am comfortable with the technical side: setting out, quantities, quality checks, reading drawings.

What I find harder is everything else. Getting subcontractor foremen who are twenty years older than me to take my instructions seriously. Knowing when to escalate a problem and when to solve it myself. Speaking up in coordination meetings when senior people disagree.

My manager is supportive, but very busy, and I do not want to ask him about every small situation.

So my question is simple: what is one skill you wish you had learned earlier, when you were a young site engineer? And how did you eventually learn it?

I would appreciate any advice, especially from people who have moved from site roles into project leadership.

authorRole: COO of a regional third-party logistics provider
post:
An uncomfortable truth about hybrid work in our industry: it is creating two classes of employee.

About 80% of our people work in warehouses, at ports or on the road. They cannot work from home. Their shifts are fixed, often at night, and swapping a shift needs a supervisor's approval days in advance.

Our office teams, meanwhile, now have two or three days at home each week and flexible hours. That is a reasonable policy for their roles. But I hear the resentment every time I visit a site: "Head office works from home while we carry the business."

I don't think the answer is to take flexibility away from office staff. I think we have been lazy about what flexibility could mean for frontline teams. Shift-swapping apps that don't need a manager's sign-off. Self-rostering within limits. Compressed weeks. Guaranteed notice of schedules.

We have started piloting some of these at two sites. Early signs are good, but it is much harder than writing a hybrid policy for the office.

HR and operations leaders: what does flexibility look like for your frontline teams?

authorRole: HR Business Partner at a manufacturing company in Malaysia
post:
I would really value advice from HR and operations leaders on this.

At our plants, most supervisors are promoted from the production floor. They are usually our best operators: reliable, skilled and respected. And roughly half of them leave, or ask to step back, within their first year as supervisors. That is about twice the rate of any other group.

Exit conversations tell a consistent story. They were not prepared for managing friends. They feel stuck between management and the floor. They find performance conversations especially hard, and some avoid them entirely until a problem becomes serious.

Our current support is a two-day leadership course and a handbook. Clearly, it is not enough.

I am considering a few options: a buddy system with experienced supervisors, monthly peer sessions without managers present, and a shorter, more practical course focused on difficult conversations.

If you have built a good programme for first-time frontline supervisors, what made the biggest difference? And what did you try that did not work?

authorRole: People Analytics Lead at a regional e-commerce company
post:
We analysed two years of performance ratings, about 4,000 in total, and found a pattern we cannot ignore.

Employees whose manager worked mostly from a different location were rated, on average, 0.3 points lower on our five-point scale than colleagues in similar roles who sat with their manager. The gap held after controlling for tenure, role level and team.

It was largest for people in their first two years, and for those in operations roles, where much of the work is not visible on a screen.

We do not think the remote employees were performing worse. Their output measures, where we had them, were similar. The more likely explanation is proximity bias: managers rate what they see.

We are trying three things this cycle. Managers write down specific examples for each rating before calibration. Calibration panels now ask, explicitly, whether location may have affected a rating. And managers of distributed teams get a short monthly template to record contributions as they happen.

I would be interested to hear whether others have looked at this in their own data, and what has helped.

authorRole: Chief People Officer at a shipping company
post:
Two years ago we stopped using forced ranking in performance reviews. Here is what happened, including the parts that did not go well.

Under the old system, every team had to place 10% of people in the lowest rating. Managers hated it, and so did employees. In practice, teams rotated the low rating from person to person each year, or gave it to whoever had just resigned.

When we removed the distribution, three things happened.

The quality of conversations improved quickly. Managers spent less time negotiating ratings in calibration and more time on what each person needed.

Ratings inflated. In the first year, almost 80% of people were rated "exceeds expectations". That made the rating far less useful to anyone.

Some managers avoided difficult conversations entirely, because there was no longer a system forcing them.

So we added guidance rather than quotas: clear descriptions for each rating with real examples, and calibration focused on evidence rather than distribution. We also trained managers specifically on giving honest feedback.

Year two looks healthier. Not perfect.

For people leaders who have made a similar change: what did you put in place of the curve?

authorRole: Regional Operations Director at a courier company
post:
For three years, I was the manager people left.

I did not realise it at the time. My depot had excellent numbers: on-time deliveries, cost per parcel, safety. I was promoted twice. My team turned over at nearly twice the regional average, and I put it down to the nature of the work.

Then one of my supervisors resigned and, in her exit conversation, told HR that she had never once had a conversation with me that was not about targets. HR shared it with me, kindly but directly.

It stung. And she was right. I knew every route and every vehicle. I did not know that she was studying part-time, or that she had wanted to move into planning for two years.

What I changed was simple. A monthly one-to-one with each supervisor, where we do not discuss the numbers for the first fifteen minutes. A question I now ask every time: what is getting in the way? And I ask supervisors to tell me about their people, not just their results.

Turnover in my region has come down noticeably since. I wish I had learned this ten years earlier.

What made you change as a manager?

authorRole: Chief Product Officer at a cross-border payments company
post:
Compliance teams that only say no are usually the product of product teams that only ask at the end.

I have been on both sides of this. Earlier in my career, I saw compliance as the final gate before launch. We would build for months, then send a finished feature for review, and get frustrated when it came back with questions we could no longer answer cheaply.

That frustration was our fault. By the time compliance saw the work, every decision had been made. The only things they could do were approve, delay or refuse.

At my current company we changed the order. A compliance partner joins every new product initiative at the problem-definition stage. They see early sketches, not final screens. They help us decide which markets to start in, which customer segments carry more risk, and what evidence we need to collect from the start.

Launch delays from late compliance findings have almost disappeared. More surprisingly, some of our best product ideas came from compliance, because they understood customer risk better than we did.

Product and compliance leaders: what has helped your teams work together earlier?

authorRole: Money Laundering Reporting Officer at a digital bank
post:
We reduced false positives in our transaction monitoring by about 60% last year. We did it by retiring rules, not by adding AI.

When I joined, we had more than 300 active monitoring rules. Many had been added after a specific incident or audit finding and never reviewed since. Analysts were closing thousands of alerts a month, most of them within minutes, because they had seen the same harmless pattern a hundred times.

We reviewed every rule against three questions. What risk does it address? When did it last produce an alert that led to a report? Does another rule already cover the same behaviour?

About a third of the rules failed all three tests and were retired. Others were merged, or retuned with better thresholds by customer segment.

Alert volumes fell sharply. More importantly, the proportion of alerts that led to a suspicious transaction report roughly tripled, and analysts finally had time to investigate properly.

We are now looking at machine learning models, but on top of a clean rule set, not as a replacement for basic hygiene.

What has worked for other compliance teams in reducing alert noise?

authorRole: Co-founder of an SME lending start-up
post:
Slightly controversial take: early-stage fintechs should not hire a full-time Head of Compliance before Series B.

Hear me out. At seed and Series A, you are still finding product-market fit. Your product may change completely within a year. A senior full-time compliance hire is a big commitment, and many candidates come from large banks, where the instinct is to build a framework designed for a much bigger organisation.

What we did instead: we used an experienced external compliance adviser two days a week and a specialist law firm for licensing questions, and gave one of our operations managers ownership of day-to-day compliance tasks, with proper training.

It worked for us for the first two years. We got our licence, passed our first audit and kept our costs manageable.

I accept the risks. External advisers are not in every product conversation, and some decisions were made without them that we later had to revisit.

But I think founders are often told to over-build compliance too early, and it slows learning.

Compliance leaders, I expect you will disagree. Where do you think the line should be?

authorRole: Compliance training manager at a regional bank
post:
A question for compliance and risk people: what is the clearest policy you have ever read?

Not the most comprehensive. Not the one that passed audit with the fewest comments. The one a new joiner could read once and know what to do.

I ask because I am leading a project to rewrite our core policies, and I keep running into the same problem. Our policies are written to satisfy reviewers, regulators and auditors. They are accurate and complete. They are also forty pages long, full of cross-references and defined terms, and very few people outside compliance read them.

Some things I am considering: a one-page summary at the front of each policy, written for the people who have to follow it. Examples of what to do in real situations. Separating "what you must do" from "why we must do it". Testing each draft with someone from the front line before approval.

I would love to hear from people who have done this well. What made a policy genuinely clear? And how did you get it through governance without it growing back to forty pages?
